author: Mark Hibben
title: Rethink Technology business briefs for January 31, 2018.
text:
Rethink Technology business briefs for January 31, 2018.
The Foxconn December bump 
Hon Hai's monthly revenue report. Source: Hon Hai . 
Rumors continue to emanate from Apple's ( AAPL ) supply chain to the effect that iPhone X sales were “disappointing”, and production in calendar Q1 is being dramatically slashed. Rather than rely on supply chain rumors, I prefer to focus on hard facts. One of the most important sources of facts that I use is monthly revenue reported by Hon Hai Precision Industries (Foxconn), which is the most important contract manufacturer for Apple. Fortunately, Hon Hai reports its revenue on a monthly basis and already has reported revenue for all three months of calendar Q4.
A very interesting thing happened in December. Hon Hai's revenue for the month jumped 50% y/y, as shown above. To see how unusual this is, I plot the monthly revenue of Hon Hai, converted to US dollars at the current exchange rate, for 2016 and 2017.
I'm reasonably certain that all of the revenue delta in November and December is attributable to iPhone X production. As a new and difficult to manufacture device, Apple would have entrusted iPhone X production exclusively to Hon Hai.
On the basis of Hon Hai's revenue bump, I estimate that Apple sold approximately 16 million iPhone Xs in the December quarter, for revenue of $17.2 billion. This puts the rumored production cut back to 20 million in calendar Q1 into perspective. If Apple sells 20 million iPhone Xs, this represents a net increase compared to calendar Q4, and a 16.6% cutback in production compared to a 24 million/quarter run rate.
My projections for sales and EPS Although some may see the 16 million in iPhone X sales as a disappointment, I believe that iPhone X sales have been largely additive to normal iPhone December revenue. Based on Hon Hai's calendar Q4 revenue, which has been closely correlated with iPhone sales for the past few years, I have concluded that iPhone revenue will be about $70.3 billion, a y/y increase of 29%. iPhone unit sales will be 88.9 million, a y/y increase of 13.55%. Although iPhone X unit sales are estimated to be about 18% of the total, iPhone X should account for about 25% of total iPhone revenue. Based on these assumptions, I estimate the iPhone ASP to be about $790.

The US government wades into the iPhone throttling controversy I continue to be absolutely appalled by the tech media coverage of the iPhone throttling controversy. I have previously described the roll of throttling in mobile device power management. It's an essential part of modern mobile device power management that occurs on a daily basis in virtually every smartphone and tablet.
Yet, the media seem embarked on a pretense that they had no idea this was going on, that goes beyond willful ignorance. Throttling has become the weapon of choice with which to beat up Apple in the eyes of consumers.
It seems a deliberate exploitation of understandable popular ignorance of the details of power management in smartphone processors. That the average consumer doesn't understand or care about those details is perfectly understandable. But to exploit that ignorance simply to make Apple look bad is unconscionable.
The latest example of this is the Bloomberg report that the US Justice Department and the SEC are “investigating” Apple. A formal investigation by these agencies is a big deal, but I doubt we're anywhere close to that.
Apple has confirmed that it received some questions from the government and is working on answering them. According to the Bloomberg report, “investigators are concerned that the company may have misled investors about the performance of older phones.”
Seriously? OK, I guess I shouldn't expect the attorneys at the DOJ and SEC to have any better technical understanding of the issue than the average consumer. But they might have asked around, rather than rely on media coverage. The government certainly has plenty of technical experts in its employ.
AMD's GPU standstill Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) was able to show substantial progress in its 2017 Q4 earnings report . AMD reported a 33% y/y gain in revenue to $1.48 billion for the quarter, and positive GAAP net income of $61 million compared to the year ago loss of $51 million.
Overall, fiscal 2017 was a substantial improvement, with a nearly 25% y/y increase in revenue to $5.33 billion and GAAP net income of $43 million, compared to the year ago loss of $497 million.
Much of the credit for this should go to CTO Mark Papermaster, who executed a brilliant strategy to bring AMD into rough parity with Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ) in x86 processors. Papermaster's resourcefulness in using multi-chip modules to create high core count processors may well become the model for the industry.
Threadripper and EPYC build on a simple 8-core silicon slice to create high core count processors by putting multiple slices into a single package. This allowed AMD to develop competitive processors on a shoestring.
The same could not be said for AMD's Vega GPUs. Despite being endowed with High Bandwidth Memory 2 (HBM2) Vega was never really competitive with Nvidia's ( NVDA ) year-old Pascal architecture, especially in energy efficiency. The net result was that AMD's progress in increasing market share ground to a halt in 2017 and actually began to reverse. This can be seen in data from Jon Peddie Research :
Perhaps the most compelling statement regarding AMD's competitive prospects in GPUs already has been made by Raja Koduri. His defection to Intel in November 2017 spoke volumes about AMD's GPU future. GPUs, like other advanced computer processors, require upwards of a billion dollars a year to develop. In its fiscal 2017 (ending January 2017), Nvidia spent $1.4 billion on R&D. In contrast, AMD spent $264 million in its fiscal 2016 (ending December 2016).
And this R&D was divided among a number of platform development projects, including Ryzen, Vega, and EPYC. It must have frustrated Koduri immensely that AMD simply didn't have the funds to realize his vision for GPUs. In light of those limited funds, it's impressive that Vega, released in 2017, got as close as it did to the performance of Nvidia's Pascal architecture GPUs, released in 2016.
To some degree, AMD was able to take advantage of Nvidia's own pause in GPU development, in which it continued to offer updates to Pascal GPUs rather than an all-new architecture in the consumer space.
Volta was a different story altogether, as Nvidia effectively slammed the door in the face of AMD's ambitions for Vega in the datacenter. Volta was the handwriting on the wall for Koduri. Nvidia could outspend and outdevelop AMD in GPUs for the foreseeable future. Nothing that Koduri could do at AMD would change that.
With Koduri's departure, AMD's progress in consumer graphics appears to have ground to a halt. As detailed in its CES press conference , there will be no new graphics architecture this year for consumer add-in boards. In fact, there will not even be the incremental improvement that's being planned for Zen based CPUs, as shown below.

The presentation graphics leave the time frames a little vague. As Anandtech clarifies in its article , Zen+ parts based on an improved Global Foundries 14 nm process, which it also calls “12 nm, ” will be what AMD ships in 2018. Zen 2 will not ship until 2019. Anandtech also made clear that Vega will not even receive the incremental performance improvements offered by the “12 nm” process, but will move directly to 7 nm.
And the Vega on 7 nm which is planned for later in 2018 will only be sampled to select customers. Navi, which would have been the answer to Nvidia's dominance of high-end GPUs, has been delayed until 2019 at the earliest.
This is clearly the result of Global Foundries' process strategy. Late in 2016, Global Foundries announced that it would skip the 10 nm node in order to proceed directly to 7 nm. GloFo claimed it would be in production of 7 nm parts by the second half of 2018. As recently as June of last year, GloFo was still assuring the world that it would be in volume production by 2018 H2.
But it's apparent from AMD's processor roadmaps that GloFo will miss its production target for 7 nm, falling behind the rest of the industry once again, as foundry leader TSMC ( TSM ) brings its 7 nm process into full production by Q2 of this year.
Nvidia, on the other hand, suffers from no such process impediment, since it relies on TSMC. Nor does it suffer from AMD's lack of cash, and I believe that a new GPU architecture will be revealed at the next GPU Technology Conference , which will be held in March. It would be logical for Nvidia to introduce a new consumer GPU architecture, considering that they didn't last year. This will probably be on a new TSMC node, either TSMC's own “12 nm” node or 10 nm.
Nvidia's new GPU architecture will be devastating to AMD in the consumer GPU space, while it continues to cement its lead in datacenter GPUs. While Intel and AMD slug it out in x86, I consider Nvidia by far the best investment of the three and remain long Nvidia.
This Tech Brief contained excerpts from longer, more detailed articles published exclusively for Rethink Technology subscribers, Nvidia Gains Substantial Desktop GPU Market Share In Q3 , and Nvidia: AMD Offers Weak Competition In 2018 .
